description: Welcome to The Hottest Here! 🔥 (Tracking urban heat anomalies). For the "Earth System Trend Detective" challenge, we’re building The Thermal Divide. Data centers dump massive waste heat while nearby neighborhoods struggle with winter energy bills. We’re using NASA data to track this heat and building a spatial routing dashboard to pipe it directly into municipal heating networks. We aren't just mapping a problem; we're building a tool to fight climate change and social inequity.
summary: The Thermal Divide is a trend detective for data-centre heat. Data centres turn almost all their electricity into waste heat, while nearby households pay to heat their homes. Using NASA MODIS land surface temperature (2016–2026), our app compares each data-centre zone with a 5–10 km ring around it, removes seasons, and tests trends with Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope. Comparing zone with ring also cancels a false clue: Terra’s orbit drift. In Melbourne, Ashburn and Dublin, data-centre zones run 0.7–1.5 °C warmer by day than their surroundings, and in Ashburn and Dublin the night-time gap is growing. NASA MERRA-2 winter heating demand then shows where that waste heat could be useful: Melbourne’s NEXTDC M3 could in theory warm about 95,000 homes. A guided case file, a Trend Lab and a heat-routing view make the analysis usable by planners, regulators and residents.
details:
What it does and how it works

The Thermal Divide is a “trend detective” for data-centre heat. Data centres turn almost all the electricity they use into waste heat, and global data-centre demand is expected to roughly double from 415 TWh (2024) to about 945 TWh by 2030 (IEA). Meanwhile, households nearby pay to heat their homes every winter. Our web app asks two questions: does that heat show up from space, and could it be put to use?

  1. Detect the heat. We downloaded NASA MODIS Terra land surface temperature (MOD11A2 v061, 8-day, 1 km) through NASA AppEEARS for three data-centre hubs: Melbourne (NEXTDC M3), Ashburn, Virginia (“Data Center Alley”) and Dublin (Grange Castle). We kept only good-quality pixels. Then we compared a 2.5 km zone around each site with a 5–10 km ring around it.
  2. Test the trend like a scientist. We removed the seasonal cycle and tested each trend with Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope, correcting for autocorrelation (method adapted from Acker et al., 2009). Every result shows a p-value and a 95% confidence range. For Melbourne, the app also compares the gap before and after M3 opened in October 2022.
  3. Link it to winter demand. NASA POWER (MERRA-2) gives heating degree-days and winter temperatures for each city. A routing view then shows how captured waste heat could reach nearby suburbs through heat pumps and a heat network.

What we found

  • Warmer zones: all three data-centre zones run warmer by day than their surroundings. Ashburn is +1.5 °C, Dublin +0.8 °C and Melbourne +0.7 °C, and all three are statistically significant.
  • Growing night gaps: in Ashburn and Dublin, the night-time gap is growing by about 0.25 °C per decade.
  • A false clue caught: raw daytime temperatures appear to fall since 2020, but that’s caused by the Terra satellite’s orbit drift. Comparing each zone with its ring cancels the drift.
  • M3 before and after: Melbourne’s gap didn’t change significantly after M3 opened. The area was already warmer, and there are only about 3 years of data since. We report this honestly.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Planners and councils: see where waste heat and heating demand overlap, as a first step toward district heating.
  • Regulators: get a free, repeatable way to monitor data-centre heat. Virginia passed HB323 in 2026, which directs the state to speed up reuse of data-centre waste heat. In Ireland, data centres used 22% of metered electricity in 2024 (CSO).
  • Operators: get evidence for heat-reuse partnerships. In theory, M3’s winter waste heat could warm about 95,000 Melbourne homes.
  • Residents and students: a guided 9-step “case file” explains the whole analysis in plain language.

Our goal is to turn data-centre waste heat from a hidden local cost into a visible, usable resource, using only free NASA data, so any city can repeat the analysis.

Tools and technologies

  • NASA data: MODIS MOD11A2 v061 via AppEEARS; NASA POWER (MERRA-2 reanalysis).
  • Data processing: Python with NumPy, rasterio, Pillow, Matplotlib and Requests. Our own statistics module handles deseasonalising, Mann-Kendall, Sen’s slope, t-tests and confidence intervals.
  • Web app: JavaScript with React 18 and Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet / React-Leaflet maps, Framer Motion and Lucide icons. It also builds as an offline single file that works without internet.
  • Base map: © Esri, HERE, Garmin, OpenStreetMap contributors.
  • Hardware: personal laptops only. No special hardware.
  • Use of SI: code and fact-checking were assisted by Claude (Anthropic). Claude also helped lay out the slide graphics from our text and results. The team chose the question, cities and data, wrote the slide content and reviewed every result. All heat maps and charts come from NASA data.

How it’s creative

  • Turns a problem into a resource: most heat-island studies stop at “it’s hotter”. We connect the heat to who could use it, and show it on a map.
  • Satellite meets policy: each city tells a different story. Melbourne has the heat supply, Virginia made heat reuse law, and Dublin shows what happens with no plan.
  • Built-in honesty: the app shows “not significant” when a result isn’t significant, catches the orbit-drift false clue, and labels every number from an example scenario as illustrative.

Factors the team considered

  • What the satellite actually measures: land surface temperature is the ground, not the air. 1 km pixels also include other industry near the data centres.
  • A fair baseline: we used a full ring around each site rather than a single comparison point. Even so, Melbourne’s city centre (~9 km away) and Dulles Airport near Ashburn sit inside the rings.
  • Satellite artefacts: Terra’s orbit drift since 2020, plus cloud and quality filtering.
  • Statistical power: only about 3 years of data exist since M3 opened.
  • Realistic claims: the 95,000-homes figure is a theoretical maximum. It needs heat pumps and a heat network, and costs depend on pipe distance.
  • Accessibility: plain-language explanations, a guided tour, and an offline version.
